samf-senior-2015-r2-03.title: Split at 12:00
samf-senior-2015-r2-03.body:
From 11:45 to 12:00 is $15$ minutes, and from 12:00 to 12:12 is $12$ minutes. Total $27$.

**Answer: 27**

samf-senior-2015-r2-04.title: Equation
samf-senior-2015-r2-04.body:
If he broke $n$ eggs, he sorted $1000-n$ unbroken eggs: $0.20(1000-n)-n=176$, so $200-1.2n=176$, $n=20$.

**Answer: 20**

samf-senior-2015-r2-04.title: Compare with no breakages
samf-senior-2015-r2-04.body:
With no breakages he would earn R200. Each broken egg loses R0.20 he would have earned plus R1 he pays: R1.20. The shortfall is $200-176=24$ rand, and $24/1.2=20$.

**Answer: 20**

samf-senior-2015-r2-05.title: Pack the books upright
samf-senior-2015-r2-05.body:
Stand the books so their $20$ cm side is vertical, exactly the height of the box. The $15$ cm side fits twice into $30$ cm and the $6$ cm side fits six times into $36$ cm. That packs $2\times6=12$ books, filling the box completely.

**Answer: 12**

samf-senior-2015-r2-05.title: Volume bound
samf-senior-2015-r2-05.body:
Box volume $=36\cdot30\cdot20=21600$ and book volume $=20\cdot15\cdot6=1800$. At most $21600/1800=12$ books fit, and the packing above reaches $12$.

**Answer: 12**

samf-senior-2015-r2-06.title: Subtract the routes through C
samf-senior-2015-r2-06.body:
The grid is $4$ wide and $3$ high, so all routes number $\binom{7}{3}=35$. Put $A=(0,0)$; then $C=(2,2)$. Routes through $C$: $\binom{4}{2}=6$ ways from $A$ to $C$ times $\binom{3}{1}=3$ ways from $C$ to $B=(4,3)$, i.e. $18$. So $35-18=17$.

**Answer: 17**

samf-senior-2015-r2-06.title: Label the intersections
samf-senior-2015-r2-06.body:
Label every intersection with the number of ways to reach it, using $0$ at $C$. From the bottom row up: $1,1,1,1,1$; then $1,2,3,4,5$; then $1,3,0,4,9$; finally $1,4,4,8,17$. So $B$ is labelled $17$.

**Answer: 17**

samf-senior-2015-r2-07.title: Weigh the columns
samf-senior-2015-r2-07.body:
Let $H,T,U$ be the sums of the hundreds, tens and units digits. The total is $100H+10T+U=99H+9T+45$ (as $H+T+U=45$), so we minimise $11H+T$. Always $H\ge1+2+3=6$. If $H\ge7$ then, since the three tens digits are distinct and each is larger than two other digits, $T\ge3+4+5=12$, so $11H+T\ge89$. If $H=6$ the hundreds digits are $1,2,3$ and the tens and units come from $4,\dots,9$. Each tens digit exceeds its units digit, so the smallest tens digit is at least $5$, the middle one is at least $7$ (three digits of $4,\dots,9$ lie below it) and the largest is $9$: $T\ge21$, giving $11H+T\ge87$, attained by tens $5,7,9$ and units $4,6,8$, e.g. $154+276+398$. The sum is $99\cdot6+9\cdot21+45=828$.

**Answer: 828**

samf-senior-2015-r2-08.title: Subtract the remainder
samf-senior-2015-r2-08.body:
$n$ divides $144-11=133=7\times19$ and $220-11=209=11\times19$. So $n$ divides $19$ and also is larger than the remainder $11$: $n=19$.

**Answer: 19**

samf-senior-2015-r2-08.title: Use the difference
samf-senior-2015-r2-08.body:
$n$ divides $220-144=76=4\times19$, so $n\in\{1,2,4,19,38,76\}$. It must exceed $11$, and $144-11=133$ is not divisible by $38$ or $76$, but $133=7\times19$. So $n=19$.

**Answer: 19**

samf-senior-2015-r2-09.title: Upper bound and packing
samf-senior-2015-r2-09.body:
Each shape covers $5$ squares and the board has $64$, so at most $\lfloor64/5\rfloor=12$ shapes fit. Two shapes together fill a $5\times2$ rectangle, so four such rectangles ($8$ shapes) cover a $5\times8$ part of the board. The remaining $3\times8$ part is two $3\times4$ blocks; in each block two shapes fit (one along the top row plus the square below one end, the other along the bottom row plus the square above the other end), leaving the two middle squares empty. That is $8+4=12$ shapes.

**Answer: 12**

samf-senior-2015-r2-10.title: Sum of squares
samf-senior-2015-r2-10.body:
The $n\times n$ pyramid is the $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ pyramid resting on a layer of $n^2$ balls, so it contains $1^2+2^2+\cdots+n^2$ balls ($1,5,14,30$ agree). For $n=10$: $1+4+9+16+25+36+49+64+81+100=385$.

**Answer: 385**

samf-senior-2015-r2-11.title: Exterior angles
samf-senior-2015-r2-11.body:
The four lines enclose a quadrilateral. At each of its four corners the two marked angles are vertically opposite, and each equals the exterior angle of the quadrilateral at that corner. So the sum of the eight angles is twice the sum of the four exterior angles, which is $2\times360=720$.

**Answer: 720**

samf-senior-2015-r2-12.title: Diophantine equation
samf-senior-2015-r2-12.body:
We need $25x+9y=839$ with $x>y$. Mod $9$: $25x\equiv7x\equiv839\equiv2\pmod 9$, so $x\equiv2\cdot4=8\pmod 9$ (as $7\cdot4=28\equiv1$). So $x=8,17,26,35,\dots$ and $y=(839-25x)/9$: $x=26$ gives $y=21<26$ (valid); $x=17$ gives $y=46>17$ (not allowed); $x=35$ gives $y<0$. So $y=21$.

**Answer: 21**

samf-senior-2015-r2-12.title: Start near equal numbers
samf-senior-2015-r2-12.body:
If $x=y$ then $34x=839$ gives $x\approx24.7$. Writing $x=24+s$, $y=24-t$ gives $25s-9t=23$, solved by $s=2$, $t=3$: $x=26$, $y=21$.

**Answer: 21**

samf-senior-2015-r2-13.title: Fill in the square
samf-senior-2015-r2-13.body:
Let the bottom right square be $x$. Then $k=31+28+x=59+x$. The anti-diagonal gives the centre as $k-33-31=x-5$. In a $3\times3$ magic square the centre is $k/3$ (the four lines through it sum to $4k$ and cover the square plus three extra centres). So $x-5=(59+x)/3$, giving $2x=74$, $x=37$ and $k=96$.

**Answer: 96**

samf-senior-2015-r2-14.title: Periodicity
samf-senior-2015-r2-14.body:
For any $n$, $x_n+x_{n+1}+x_{n+2}+x_{n+3}=30=x_{n+1}+x_{n+2}+x_{n+3}+x_{n+4}$, so $x_n=x_{n+4}$: the contents repeat every $4$ boxes. $2015=4\cdot503+3$, so box $2015$ has the same number as box $3$, which is $7$.

**Answer: 7**

samf-senior-2015-r2-15.title: Two congruent triangles under D
samf-senior-2015-r2-15.body:
Let the sides of $C$, $D$, $E$ be $c,d,e$. The lower-left side of $D$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with vertical leg $c$ (the right side of $C$) and a horizontal leg $w$. The corner of $D$ on the line is a right angle, so the triangle under the lower-right side of $D$, with vertical leg $e$ (the left side of $E$), has the same hypotenuse $d$ and complementary acute angles. The two triangles are therefore congruent and $w=e$. Pythagoras gives $d^2=c^2+e^2$. With $c^2=16$ and $d^2=2\cdot20=40$ we get $e^2=24$, the area of $E$.

**Answer: 24**

samf-senior-2015-r2-16.title: Add the four sums
samf-senior-2015-r2-16.body:
Each number appears in three of the four sums, so $20+22+24+27=93=3S$ where $S$ is the total of the four numbers. Hence $S=31$.

**Answer: 31**

samf-senior-2015-r2-18.title: Widths and heights
samf-senior-2015-r2-18.body:
Let the column widths be $w_1,w_2,w_3$ and the row heights $h_1,h_2,h_3$. Half-perimeters of the given rectangles: top-middle $w_2+h_1=9$, bottom-middle $w_2+h_3=8$, left-middle $w_1+h_2=9$, right-middle $w_3+h_2=10$, centre $w_2+h_2=11$. Adding the first four: $2w_2+2h_2+(w_1+w_3+h_1+h_3)=36$, so $w_1+w_3+h_1+h_3=36-22=14$. Then the half-perimeter of the large rectangle is $14+(w_2+h_2)=25$ and its perimeter is $50$.

**Answer: 50**

samf-senior-2015-r2-19.title: Rotate triangle DBC
samf-senior-2015-r2-19.body:
Rotate triangle $DBC$ about $D$ so that $C$ lands on $E$ (possible since $DC=DE$); $B$ goes to $B'$. Then $\angle DEB'=\angle DCB=90^\circ$, and since $\angle DEA=90^\circ$, the points $A,E,B'$ are collinear with $AB'=AE+EB'=AE+CB=AB$. Also $DB'=DB$ and $DA$ is common, so triangles $DAB'$ and $DAB$ are congruent (SSS) and $\angle ADB'=\angle ADB=180^\circ-70^\circ-60^\circ=50^\circ$. The rotation angle is $\angle EDC=\angle B'DB=\angle B'DA+\angle ADB=100^\circ$.

**Answer: 100**

samf-senior-2015-r2-20.title: Count exponent patterns
samf-senior-2015-r2-20.body:
Every product has the form $3^a4^b5^c6^d7^e$ with $0\le a\le1$, $0\le b\le2$, $0\le c\le2$, $0\le d\le1$, $0\le e\le3$. Different exponent tuples give different numbers (the exponent of $2$ is $2b+d$ and of $3$ is $a+d$; the parity of $2b+d$ gives $d$, then $b$ and $a$ follow). There are $2\cdot3\cdot3\cdot2\cdot4=144$ tuples. Remove the tuple with $a+b+c+d+e=0$ (the empty product) and the five with sum $1$ (single numbers $3,4,5,6,7$), since at least two factors are needed: $144-1-5=138$.

**Answer: 138**
